pos: v. and n. (to draw near; in the law, to come near to what is holy or forbidden; rendering Hebrew qarab, nagash, Greek proserchomai)
etymology: From Latin ad, to, and prope, near. In Leviticus the word is technical, and it governs the two things a man must not draw near to without warrant: the holy, and the forbidden.
biblical_def: Approach in the law marks a boundary. On one side stand the forbidden nearnesses of Leviticus 18: “None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD” (Lev 18:6) — the incest laws, given as a limit on approach rather than a list of feelings. On the other side stands the holy, guarded just as strictly: a priest with a blemish “shall not approach to offer the bread of his God” (Lev 21:17), and the Kohathites are given careful instruction “that they may live, and not die, when they approach unto the most holy things” (Num 4:19). Approach to God was lethal without appointment. That is the background against which Hebrews issues its astonishing invitation: “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace” (Heb 4:16). The barrier was real, the blemish disqualified, and the veil has been torn by a High Priest without blemish who approached in our stead.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines approach as to come or go near in place, to draw nigh — and notes the sense of approaching God, that is, of drawing near in worship or prayer.
webster_full: APPROACH, v.i. To come or go near, in place; to draw near; to advance nearer.
2. To draw near in time.
3. To draw near, in a figurative sense; to advance near to a point aimed at.
4. To draw near in duty, as in prayer or worship. They take delight in approaching to God. Is. lviii.
scriptures: Heb 4:16
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
Speak unto Aaron, saying, Whosoever he be of thy seed in their generations that hath any blemish, let him not approach to offer the bread of his God.
Num 4:19
But thus do unto them, that they may live, and not die, when they approach unto the most holy things: Aaron and his sons shall go in, and appoint them every one to his service and to his burden:
Lev 18:6
None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD.
corruption_summary: Access to God assumed as a natural right, so that boldness at the throne is mistaken for casualness — the veil forgotten along with the fact that it had to be torn.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern devotional habit begins where Hebrews 4:16 ends and skips everything that made it necessary. Numbers 4:19 exists so that men handling the most holy things “may live, and not die”; Leviticus 21 bars a blemished priest from approaching at all. Boldness at the throne of grace is therefore not a natural entitlement but a purchased anomaly, and a prayer life that has never felt the weight of the barrier will not feel the wonder of its removal either. Reverence and boldness are not opposites in Scripture; boldness is what reverence does once the way is opened.

Leviticus 18 makes the same word govern the other kind of nearness. The incest and adultery laws are framed as limits on approach, repeatedly punctuated with I am the LORD — the prohibitions are grounded in God's character rather than in social convention or consequence. An age that reasons about sexual ethics entirely from consent has no category for a nearness that is wrong simply because God has fixed a boundary there, and Leviticus 18:6 supplies precisely that category.
roots_summary: Hebrew qarab (H7126), to come near, approach — the root of korban, an offering; nagash (H5066), to draw near; Greek proserchomai (G4334), to come to — Hebrews' word for drawing near to God.
roots_lines: Hebrew qarab (H7126) — to draw near, approach; the same root gives korban, the offering by which approach was made possible.
Hebrew nagash (H5066) — to come near, especially to God or to a superior; used of Abraham drawing near to intercede for Sodom (Gen 18:23).
Greek proserchomai (G4334) — to come toward; Hebrews' repeated invitation to draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith (Heb 10:22).
usage: “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace” — boldness as a purchased anomaly.
“That they may live, and not die, when they approach unto the most holy things”.
“None of you shall approach… I am the LORD” — a boundary grounded in God's character.

pos: v. (to trip in walking; figuratively, to fall into sin or error; rendering Hebrew kashal, Greek proskopto, ptaio)
etymology: From Old Norse stumra, to grope. To stumble is to lose footing without necessarily falling — and Scripture attends closely to the difference.
biblical_def: Stumble is Scripture's ordinary word for a misstep in the walk, and Proverbs makes it the plain promise attached to wisdom: “Then shalt thou walk in thy way safely, and thy foot shall not stumble” (Pro 3:23); “when thou runnest, thou shalt not stumble” (Pro 4:12). The corresponding description of the wicked is one of the bleakest lines in the book: “The way of the wicked is as darkness: they know not at what they stumble” (Pro 4:19) — not merely that they fall, but that they cannot identify the cause, which is the definition of a life without light. Hannah's song promises reversal to those who have already gone down: “they that stumbled are girded with strength” (1Sa 2:4). And Proverbs forbids the natural pleasure at an enemy's misstep: “Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth” (Pro 24:17) — a command aimed at the heart, not merely the mouth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stumble as to trip in walking or moving in any way upon the legs, to strike the foot so as to fall or endanger a fall — and figuratively, to err, to slide into crime or error.
webster_full: STUM´BLE, v.i. To trip in walking or moving in any way upon the legs; to strike the foot so as to fall, or to endanger a fall.
2. To err; to slide into crime or error.
He that loveth his brother, abideth in the light, and there is none occasion of stumbling in him. 1 John ii.
3. To strike upon without design; to fall on; to light on by chance.
scriptures: Pro 4:19
The way of the wicked is as darkness: they know not at what they stumble.
Pro 3:23
Then shalt thou walk in thy way safely, and thy foot shall not stumble.
The bows of the mighty men are broken, and they that stumbled are girded with strength.
Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth:
corruption_summary: A stumble treated as a fall — despair after sin, as though a misstep ended the walk — and the private satisfaction at an enemy's stumble left entirely unrepented.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pastoral error is collapsing stumbling into falling. Proverbs promises the righteous man that his foot shall not stumble, and Scripture elsewhere says a just man falleth seven times and riseth up again — so the promise plainly does not mean an unbroken record. It means a walk that is not brought to an end by a misstep. Jude's doxology names the true guarantor: him that is able to keep you from falling (Jud 1:24). The keeping is God's, and it is compatible with a great deal of stumbling.

The neglected command is Proverbs 24:17. Rejoicing when an enemy stumbles is so instinctive that it is rarely even confessed, and the verse forbids it at the level of the heart — let not thine heart be glad. That closes the usual escape, which is to say nothing while enjoying it thoroughly. And Proverbs 4:19 supplies the sober counterweight: the wicked stumble in the dark and cannot tell what tripped them. To know what one has stumbled over is already a mercy.
roots_summary: Hebrew kashal (H3782), to totter, stumble, be feeble; Greek proskopto (G4350), to strike against; ptaio (G4417), to trip — the verb behind able to keep you from falling.
roots_lines: Hebrew kashal (H3782) — to stumble, totter, be brought low; those that stumbled girded with strength (1Sa 2:4).
Greek proskomma (G4348) — a stumbling-block; Christ Himself is a stone of stumbling to unbelief (1Pe 2:8).
Greek ptaio (G4417) — to trip, stumble, err; in many things we offend all (Jas 3:2), and yet He is able to keep from falling (Jud 1:24).
usage: “They know not at what they stumble” — the definition of a life without light.
“Thy foot shall not stumble” — a walk not ended by a misstep.
“Let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth” — aimed at the heart, not the mouth.

pos: v. (to move downward; used pre-eminently of God coming down; rendering Hebrew yarad, Greek katabaino)
etymology: From Latin de, down, and scandere, to climb. In Scripture the direction is the doctrine: religion climbs, and God descends.
biblical_def: Descend is one of the great theological verbs of the Bible, because in Scripture the decisive movement is always downward. God descends on Sinai: “mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, because the LORD descended upon it in fire” (Exo 19:18). He descends to the tent: “as Moses entered into the tabernacle, the cloudy pillar descended, and stood at the door” (Exo 33:9). He descends to proclaim His own name: “the LORD descended in the cloud, and stood with him there, and proclaimed the name of the LORD” (Exo 34:5). And Jacob's ladder shows the traffic in both directions — “the angels of God ascending and descending on it” (Gen 28:12) — a vision the Lord Jesus claims for Himself, making His own person the ladder. Set beside Babel, whose builders wanted a tower “whose top may reach unto heaven”, the contrast is total. Man builds up and is scattered; God comes down and dwells.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines descend as to move or pass from a higher to a lower place, to fall, to sink — and notes its use for proceeding from an original or ancestor by generation.
webster_full: DESCEND, v.i. To move or pass from a higher to a lower place; to move, come or go downwards; to fall; to sink; to run or flow down.
2. To go down, or to enter.
3. To come suddenly, or in a violent manner.
4. To proceed from a source or original; to be derived. 5. To pass from general to particular considerations.
scriptures: And mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, because the LORD descended upon it in fire: and the smoke thereof ascended as the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mount quaked greatly.
Exo 34:5
And the LORD descended in the cloud, and stood with him there, and proclaimed the name of the LORD.
And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it.
Exo 33:9
And it came to pass, as Moses entered into the tabernacle, the cloudy pillar descended, and stood at the door of the tabernacle, and the LORD talked with Moses.
corruption_summary: Religion as ascent — the ladder of technique, experience, or moral progress by which a man climbs to God — against a canon in which every decisive movement is God's descent.
corruption_paragraphs: Every man-made religion is a ladder, and the varieties are only in the rungs: ritual, moral achievement, mystical technique, or self-improvement. Babel is the archetype — a tower whose top may reach unto heaven, built to make a name — and Genesis notes with quiet irony that the LORD had to come down to see the city. Scripture's pattern is the reverse of religion's: God descends on Sinai, descends to the tabernacle door, descends in a cloud to speak His own name, and finally descends in the flesh.

Jacob's ladder is where the two meet, and the Lord Jesus settles its meaning by applying it to Himself — the angels ascending and descending on the Son of man. The ladder is not a method; it is a Person, and He is set up at the bottom where Jacob was sleeping, not at the top where he might have wished to climb. The believer's comfort in Exodus 34:5 is the same: God descended and proclaimed His own name, which means the knowledge of God is revelation received, not a summit attained.
roots_summary: Hebrew yarad (H3381), to go down, descend — used of God at Sinai, at Babel, and at the tent; Greek katabaino (G2597), to come down — of the Spirit at the baptism and of the Lord at His return.
roots_lines: Hebrew yarad (H3381) — to descend, go down; the LORD came down to see the city and the tower (Gen 11:5), and descended on Sinai in fire (Exo 19:18).
Greek katabaino (G2597) — to come down; the Spirit descending like a dove (Mat 3:16) and the Lord descending with a shout (1Th 4:16).
Greek anabaino (G305) — to ascend; paired with katabaino on Jacob's ladder and in the Lord's words to Nathanael (John 1:51).
usage: “The LORD descended upon it in fire” — the mountain came to no one; God came down.
“The LORD descended in the cloud… and proclaimed the name of the LORD” — revelation, not summit.
“The angels of God ascending and descending on it” — and the ladder is a Person.

pos: v. (to come up with in pursuit; rendering Hebrew nasag, Greek katalambano)
etymology: A plain English compound, to take over or come upon from behind. Scripture uses it for blessings and curses alike — both pictured as things that pursue a man.
biblical_def: Overtake is a pursuit word, and Deuteronomy 28 puts it to unforgettable use on both sides of the covenant. Of obedience: “all these blessings shall come on thee, and overtake thee, if thou shalt hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God” (Deu 28:2) — blessings chasing a man down, catching him from behind. Of disobedience, in identical form: “all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee” (Deu 28:15), and again, “shall pursue thee, and overtake thee, till thou be destroyed” (Deu 28:45). The same verb, the same posture, opposite contents. Pharaoh boasts it at the sea — “I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil” (Exo 15:9) — five confident first-person verbs, and the sea closes over every one. And David asks God whether pursuit is warranted, and is answered exactly: “Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all” (1Sa 30:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines overtake as to come up with in a course, pursuit or motion — and to come upon, to take by surprise, as calamity overtakes the sinner.
webster_full: OVERTA´KE, v.t. To come up with in a course, pursuit, progress or motion; to catch.
2. To come upon; to take by surprise.
Lest that day come upon you unawares. Luke xxi.
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye who are spiritual, restore such a one. Gal. vi.
scriptures: Deu 28:2
And all these blessings shall come on thee, and overtake thee, if thou shalt hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God.

But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee:
Exo 15:9
The enemy said, I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil; my lust shall be satisfied upon them; I will draw my sword, my hand shall destroy them.
And David enquired at the LORD, saying, Shall I pursue after this troop? shall I overtake them? And he answered him, Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all.
corruption_summary: Consequences imagined as escapable by distance or delay — when Deuteronomy pictures both blessing and curse as pursuers that do not tire.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 28's image is more searching than a simple statement of consequence. Blessings and curses do not merely follow from conduct; they pursue and overtake. A man may outrun them for a season, which is exactly why the delay deceives him, and the verb is chosen to say that the interval is not an escape. Nothing in modern life has changed the arithmetic; it has only lengthened the interval and multiplied the distractions inside it.

The pastoral use is the reverse and is often missed. Deuteronomy 28:2 says blessings overtake the obedient — they come from behind, unlooked-for, catching a man who was not calculating them. That forecloses the transactional reading of covenant obedience, in which a man performs and then collects. The blessings are described as pursuing him while he walks, which is a far better picture of the Christian life than a ledger. And Galatians 6:1 applies the same verb tenderly: a man overtaken in a fault is to be restored, not finished off.
roots_summary: Hebrew nasag (H5381), to reach, overtake, attain — used of pursuers and of blessings; Greek katalambano (G2638), to seize, lay hold of — also Paul's word for apprehending the prize.
roots_lines: Hebrew nasag (H5381) — to overtake, reach, be able; blessings and curses alike overtake in Deu 28.
Greek katalambano (G2638) — to lay hold of, seize; the darkness comprehended it not (John 1:5), and Paul presses to apprehend that for which he was apprehended (Php 3:12).
Greek prolambano (G4301) — to take beforehand, overtake; if a man be overtaken in a fault (Gal 6:1).
usage: “All these blessings shall come on thee, and overtake thee” — blessings as pursuers.
“Shall pursue thee, and overtake thee” — the interval is not an escape.
“I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil” — and the sea closed over him.

pos: v. (to be carried on an animal or in a vehicle; rendering Hebrew rakab, Greek epikathizo)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon ridan. In the ancient world the mount declared the man: a horse meant war, an ass meant peace, and a king's own mule meant succession.
biblical_def: Ride in Scripture is never a neutral detail, because the mount is a statement. Joseph is made to “ride in the second chariot” with heralds crying before him (Gen 41:43) — elevation announced by conveyance. Solomon is set on David's own mule to settle the succession beyond argument (1Ki 1:33). Deborah's song addresses the ruling class as “ye that ride on white asses, ye that sit in judgment” (Jdg 5:10). Most striking, the word is used of God Himself: “There is none like unto the God of Jeshurun, who rideth upon the heaven in thy help” (Deu 33:26), and He “made him ride on the high places of the earth” (Deu 32:13). All of it gathers into Zechariah's prophecy of the King who comes “lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass” (Zec 9:9) — a deliberate choice of mount, fulfilled at the triumphal entry, announcing a King who comes in peace.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ride as to be carried on horseback, or on any beast, or in any vehicle — noting the distinction between riding and driving, and the figurative sense of managing at will.
webster_full: RIDE, v.i. To be carried on horseback, or on any beast, or in any vehicle.
2. To be borne on or in a fluid; to float.
3. To be supported in motion; as, to ride on the wind.
4. To manage a horse well. RIDE, v.t. To manage insolently at will; as, a nation ridden by a tyrant.
scriptures: Zec 9:9

Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass.
There is none like unto the God of Jeshurun, who rideth upon the heaven in thy help, and in his excellency on the sky.
The king also said unto them, Take with you the servants of your lord, and cause Solomon my son to ride upon mine own mule, and bring him down to Gihon:
And he made him to ride in the second chariot which he had; and they cried before him, Bow the knee: and he made him ruler over all the land of Egypt.
corruption_summary: A Christ imagined on the war-horse first and the colt never — power expected in the form the world recognizes — when the King deliberately chose the mount of peace on the way to the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: Zechariah 9:9 is a study in chosen weakness. Everything in the ancient vocabulary of power said horse: a conquering king rode a warhorse into a taken city. The prophecy specifies an ass, and a borrowed colt at that, and the Lord Jesus arranges for it deliberately. The crowd shouting Hosanna wanted a horse and got a colt, and by Friday the same crowd wanted Him crucified. Any expectation of Christ that cannot accommodate the colt will not survive contact with the cross.

This does not deny the other picture. Deuteronomy 33:26 shows God riding upon the heaven, and Revelation shows the rider on the white horse. But the order is fixed and cannot be reversed: the colt first, then the horse; the cross before the crown. A Christianity that reaches for worldly instruments of power because they are the ones that visibly work has misread the order, and generally does not notice that it is the crowd's misreading rather than a new one.
roots_summary: Hebrew rakab (H7392), to ride, mount — used of men, kings, and of God riding the heavens; the noun rekeb is a chariot; Greek epikathizo (G1940), to sit upon.
roots_lines: Hebrew rakab (H7392) — to ride, be carried; used of God riding upon the heaven (Deu 33:26) and upon a swift cloud (Isa 19:1).
Hebrew chamor (H2543) — an ass; the mount of peace and of judges (Jdg 5:10), specified by Zechariah for the coming King.
Greek polos (G4454) — a colt; the unbroken foal on which no man had sat, loosed for the Lord's entry (Mar 11:2).
usage: “Lowly, and riding upon an ass” — the mount is the message.
“Who rideth upon the heaven in thy help” — the same verb, of God.
“Cause Solomon my son to ride upon mine own mule” — succession settled by a mount.

pos: v. (to seize, take hold of, ensnare; rendering Hebrew lakad, achaz, Greek piazo, harpazo)
etymology: From Old North French cachier, to chase, from Latin captare, to try to seize. To catch is the successful end of a chase — and in Scripture the catcher is often God.
biblical_def: Catch in Scripture is usually about who does the seizing. The most consequential instance is a ram: “behold behind him a ram caught in a thicket by his horns: and Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering in the stead of his son” (Gen 22:13) — a substitute caught and held at the exact moment it was needed, which is the whole doctrine of providence in one animal. Joseph is caught by Potiphar's wife and escapes by leaving his garment behind (Gen 39:12) — the only recorded strategy against that temptation being flight. Moses is told to catch the serpent by the tail, the least safe way to hold one, and it becomes a rod in his hand (Exo 4:4). And the law of restitution covers a fire that catches in thorns and spreads: “he that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution” (Exo 22:6) — a man is liable for what his fire catches, even where he did not intend the spread.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines catch as to seize or lay hold on with the hand, to seize in motion, to stop and hold — and to ensnare, to entangle in a snare.
webster_full: CATCH, v.t. To seize or lay hold on with the hand; to seize any thing that is moving.
2. To stop and hold; to interrupt in its course.
3. To ensnare; to entangle in a snare; as, to catch a bird or a fish.
4. To seize in a moral sense; to take hold of; to insnare. 5. To take, as a disease, by contagion.
scriptures: And Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and behold behind him a ram caught in a thicket by his horns: and Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering in the stead of his son.
And she caught him by his garment, saying, Lie with me: and he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.
Exo 4:4
And the LORD said unto Moses, Put forth thine hand, and take it by the tail. And he put forth his hand, and caught it, and it became a rod in his hand:
Exo 22:6
If fire break out, and catch in thorns, so that the stacks of corn, or the standing corn, or the field, be consumed therewith; he that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution.
corruption_summary: Providence reduced to coincidence, so that the ram in the thicket becomes luck — and, in ethics, liability denied for fires a man kindled but did not intend to spread.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 22:13 is the verse that gave the place its name: Jehovah-jireh, the LORD will provide. A ram is caught in a thicket, at the top of a mountain, at the precise moment a knife is raised — and Abraham had already told Isaac that God would provide Himself a lamb. Read as coincidence, the passage is merely a lucky escape. Read as Scripture presents it, the substitute was caught and held there by the same hand that stayed the knife, and the mountain becomes the place where the greater Substitute would be offered.

Exodus 22:6 supplies an ethic the age has largely abandoned. A man kindles a fire, it catches in thorns, and the standing corn burns: he that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution. He did not intend the spread; he is liable for it anyway. That principle governs words as much as flames, and a culture in which no one is answerable for what their kindling caught — because the intention was innocent — is at odds with the law of Moses on ordinary damages.
roots_summary: Hebrew lakad (H3920), to capture, take, ensnare; achaz (H270), to grasp, hold fast — the ram caught in the thicket; Greek harpazo (G726), to seize by force, catch away.
roots_lines: Hebrew achaz (H270) — to grasp, hold fast; the ram caught and held in the thicket (Gen 22:13).
Hebrew lakad (H3920) — to capture, take by snare or lot; the wicked taken in their own naughtiness (Pro 11:6).
Greek harpazo (G726) — to snatch, seize; Paul caught up to the third heaven (2Co 12:2) and the saints caught up in the clouds (1Th 4:17).
usage: “A ram caught in a thicket by his horns” — a substitute held in place at the hour of need.
“She caught him by his garment… and fled” — the only strategy Scripture records.
“He that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution” — liable for what it caught.

pos: v. (to draw with force; in the prophets, to pull down what is built; rendering Hebrew nathats, nathash, Greek kathaireo)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon pullian, to pluck. In the prophets pull down is a technical commission — the demolition that must precede any building.
biblical_def: Pull is force applied, and Jeremiah's call turns on it. God sets the prophet “over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant” (Jer 1:10) — four verbs of demolition to two of construction, and the demolition comes first. That order governs all genuine reformation: the high places must come down before the altar goes up. God claims the same sovereign freedom in both directions: “I will build them, and not pull them down; and I will plant them, and not pluck them up” (Jer 24:6). Jeroboam supplies the picture of a man caught mid-gesture: he stretches out his hand against the prophet, “and his hand… dried up, so that he could not pull it in again to him” (1Ki 13:4) — the arm raised against God's word frozen where it was raised. And David prays the word for rescue: “Pull me out of the net that they have laid privily for me” (Psa 31:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pull as to draw, to endeavor to move by drawing toward one — and to pull down, to demolish or to degrade.
webster_full: PULL, v.t. To draw; to endeavor to draw; to exert strength in drawing any thing toward one.
2. To pluck; to gather by drawing; as, to pull fruit.
3. To tear; to rend; as, to pull in pieces.
To pull down, to demolish or to take in pieces by separating the parts; also, to degrade; to bring from a higher to a lower state.
scriptures: Jer 1:10
See, I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant.
Jer 24:6
For I will set mine eyes upon them for good, and I will bring them again to this land: and I will build them, and not pull them down; and I will plant them, and not pluck them up.

And it came to pass, when king Jeroboam heard the saying of the man of God, which had cried against the altar in Bethel, that he put forth his hand from the altar, saying, Lay hold on him. And his hand, which he put forth against him, dried up, so that he could not pull it in again to him.
Psa 31:4
Pull me out of the net that they have laid privily for me: for thou art my strength.
corruption_summary: A ministry of demolition without building, and a building without demolition — both halves of Jeremiah's commission separated, and each half alone producing ruin.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 1:10 has six verbs, and men persistently take three. Some ministries pull down and never plant: they are expert at exposing error, and their hearers end with a demolished field and nothing growing in it. Others build and plant without ever pulling down: they raise structures on ground that was never cleared, and the old altars stand beside the new. The reformers of Judah are the test case — the ones Scripture commends most highly are the ones who removed the high places, and the qualified praise given to the rest usually turns on that exact omission.

Jeremiah 24:6 keeps the whole commission where it belongs, in God's hand. I will build them, and not pull them down. The prophet is the instrument; the sovereign decision to plant or uproot a people is not his. And 1 Kings 13:4 is the standing warning to those who raise a hand against a word they dislike: Jeroboam's arm dried up in the position he had stretched it, and he could not pull it back. He had to ask the prophet he was arresting to pray for him.
roots_summary: Hebrew nathats (H5422), to pull down, break down — used of altars and high places; nathash (H5428), to pluck up by the roots; Greek kathaireo (G2507), to take down, demolish.
roots_lines: Hebrew nathats (H5422) — to pull down, demolish; the standing verb for breaking down altars and images (Deu 7:5).
Hebrew nathash (H5428) — to pluck up, root out; paired with pull down in Jeremiah's commission (Jer 1:10; Jer 24:6).
Greek kathairesis (G2506) — a pulling down; Paul's weapons are mighty to the pulling down of strong holds (2Co 10:4).
usage: “To root out, and to pull down… to build, and to plant” — and the demolition comes first.
“I will build them, and not pull them down” — the decision is God's, not the prophet's.
“He could not pull it in again to him” — the hand frozen where it was raised.

pos: v. (to extend to, arrive at, stretch out; rendering Hebrew naga, nasag, Greek ephikneomai)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon raecan, to extend. Scripture asks repeatedly what a thing reaches to — and answers, of every human structure, that it falls short.
biblical_def: Reach asks how far a thing extends, and Scripture sets two towers side by side to answer it. Babel: “let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name” (Gen 11:4) — and the next verse has God coming down to look at it. Bethel: “a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven” (Gen 28:12) — not built, but set up, and given to a fugitive asleep on a stone. Man's tower does not reach; God's ladder does. The word also carries the covenant blessing of abundance in one of the loveliest promises of Leviticus: “your threshing shall reach unto the vintage, and the vintage shall reach unto the sowing time” (Lev 26:5) — harvests overlapping, one running into the next with no hungry gap between. And in the tabernacle it describes the hidden middle bar that “shall reach from end to end” (Exo 26:28), unseen and holding everything together.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reach as to extend, to stretch, to extend so as to touch or arrive at — and to attain to, or to arrive at by effort or motion.
webster_full: REACH, v.t. To extend; to stretch; in a general sense; as, to reach out the arm.
2. To extend to, so as to touch or place on.
3. To strike from a distance.
4. To arrive at; to come to. 5. To attain to; to gain; to obtain; as, to reach a good old age.
scriptures: Gen 11:4
And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.
And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it.
Lev 26:5
And your threshing shall reach unto the vintage, and the vintage shall reach unto the sowing time: and ye shall eat your bread to the full, and dwell in your land safely.
And the middle bar in the midst of the boards shall reach from end to end.
corruption_summary: Human reach believed unlimited — the tower's premise, that with enough coordination heaven is attainable — and the name men build for themselves preferred to the name given them.
corruption_paragraphs: Babel's builders stated their project honestly: a top that may reach unto heaven, and let us make us a name. Both halves recur in every age of technical confidence. The judgment on Babel was not that ambition is wicked in itself, but that the reach was aimed at heaven and the name was self-issued. Genesis makes the point with restraint rather than thunder: the LORD came down to see the tower whose top reached heaven, which quietly measures the distance the builders had actually covered.

Bethel answers Babel exactly. Jacob is running for his life, sleeping on a stone, having deceived his father, and God sets up a ladder whose top reaches to heaven and stands above it to speak promises. Nothing is built; nothing is earned; the name is given rather than made. That is the whole difference between religion and grace, and Genesis puts the two towers seventeen chapters apart so the reader can hold them together.
roots_summary: Hebrew naga (H5060), to touch, reach; nasag (H5381), to overtake, attain; Greek ephikneomai (G2185), to reach as far as — Paul's we reach even unto you (2Co 10:14).
roots_lines: Hebrew naga (H5060) — to touch, strike, reach; the tower's top intended to touch heaven (Gen 11:4).
Hebrew nasag (H5381) — to reach, attain, overtake; the overlapping harvests of Lev 26:5.
Greek ephikneomai (G2185) — to come upon, reach unto; Paul's measure of his own commission (2Co 10:13-14).
usage: “Whose top may reach unto heaven… let us make us a name” — and the LORD came down to see it.
“The top of it reached to heaven” — not built, but set up, and given to a fugitive.
“Your threshing shall reach unto the vintage” — harvests with no hungry gap between.

pos: n. and v. (a sheet spread to catch the wind; to travel by ship; rendering Hebrew nes, Greek pleo)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon segl. Israel was not a seafaring people, so sailing enters Scripture mainly with the gospel — and then it goes everywhere.
biblical_def: Sail is rare in the Old Testament and constant in Acts, and the shift is itself the story. Isaiah uses a failing ship to picture a helpless nation: “Thy tacklings are loosed; they could not well strengthen their mast, they could not spread the sail” (Isa 33:23) — and then, startlingly, the lame take the prey anyway. Ezekiel describes Tyre's sail of fine embroidered Egyptian linen (Eze 27:7), luxury rigged for commerce, in a lament over a city about to sink. Then Luke picks up the word and the gospel begins to move: “being sent forth by the Holy Ghost, they departed unto Seleucia; and from thence they sailed to Cyprus” (Act 13:4). Even the sharpest quarrel in the apostolic company ends under sail — “Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus” (Act 15:39) — and God turns a contention into two missions. And on the lake, while the disciples sailed, He fell asleep (Luk 8:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a sail as a spread of cloth, extended to the wind to receive its impulse and drive a vessel forward — and as a verb, to be impelled or driven forward by wind upon sails.
webster_full: SAIL, n. In navigation, a spread of canvas, or an assemblage of several breadths of canvas, sewed together with a double seam, and edged with a cord called the bolt-rope.
2. In poetry, wings.
3. A ship or other vessel; used in the singular for a single ship, or as a collective noun for a number.
SAIL, v.i. To be impelled or driven forward by the action of wind upon sails, as a ship on water.
scriptures: Act 13:4
So they, being sent forth by the Holy Ghost, departed unto Seleucia; and from thence they sailed to Cyprus.
Thy tacklings are loosed; they could not well strengthen their mast, they could not spread the sail: then is the prey of a great spoil divided; the lame take the prey.
And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other: and so Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus;
Luk 8:23
But as they sailed he fell asleep: and there came down a storm of wind on the lake; and they were filled with water, and were in jeopardy.
corruption_summary: Mission conceived as an enterprise men launch, when Acts has the Holy Ghost doing the sending — and the church's quarrels imagined as pure loss, when God has been known to sail two ships out of one.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The correction is to the grammar of mission. Acts 13:4 puts the agency plainly: being sent forth by the Holy Ghost, they sailed. The church at Antioch fasted, prayed, and laid on hands, and the text still attributes the sending to the Spirit. Where missionary work is spoken of purely as strategy, funding, and deployment, that sentence has quietly dropped out, and with it the confidence that the enterprise is not finally ours to sustain.

Acts 15:39 is the passage to hold on to when the church is at odds with itself. Paul and Barnabas disagreed sharply over Mark, and the contention was so sharp that they parted — Luke does not tidy it up or assign blame. Two ships sailed instead of one, Mark was recovered and later called profitable by Paul himself, and the mission doubled. That is not a licence for quarrelling. It is the assurance that a sovereign God is not stopped by the failures of good men.
roots_summary: Hebrew nes (H5251), a sail, ensign, banner — the same word for a standard lifted up; Greek pleo (G4126), to sail; apopleo (G636), to sail away, the recurring verb of Acts.
roots_lines: Hebrew nes (H5251) — a sail, flag, ensign; the same word for the standard lifted to the nations (Isa 11:12) and for the brasen serpent set on a pole.
Greek pleo (G4126) — to sail; used of the disciples on the lake (Luk 8:23) and repeatedly of Paul's voyages.
Greek ekpleo (G1602) — to sail out from; the departures that carried the gospel out of Asia into Europe (Act 20:6).
usage: “Being sent forth by the Holy Ghost… they sailed to Cyprus” — the agency is named.
“They could not spread the sail… the lame take the prey” — victory without seamanship.
“As they sailed he fell asleep” — the calmest man aboard.

pos: v. (to hurry, to urge forward; rendering Hebrew mahar, chush, Greek speudo)
etymology: From haste, Old French haste, speed. Scripture distinguishes sharply between hurrying toward obedience and the anxious hurry that Proverbs assigns to want.
biblical_def: Hasten in Scripture is measured by its direction. Abraham's hospitality is a flurry of it: he “hastened into the tent unto Sarah” and told her to make ready quickly, then “ran unto the herd… and he hasted to dress it” (Gen 18:6, 7) — an old man running, three times over, for three strangers. Rebekah at the well shows the same energy, hasting to empty her pitcher and running again to draw for ten camels (Gen 24:20). This is haste in the service of others, and Scripture plainly admires it. Then there is the haste of rescue: “the angels hastened Lot” (Gen 19:15) — a man who had to be hurried out of a city about to burn, and who still lingered. And the haste of the oppressor: “the taskmasters hasted them” (Exo 5:13). The same verb serves love, rescue, and tyranny, and only the object tells them apart.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hasten as to press, to drive or urge forward, to push on, to precipitate, to accelerate movement — and intransitively, to move with celerity.
webster_full: HAS´TEN, v.t. has´n. To press; to drive or urge forward; to push on; to precipitate; to accelerate movement.
HAS´TEN, v.i. To move with celerity; to be speedy or quick.
I will hasten my word to perform it. Jer. i.
Hasten, my beloved, and be thou like to a roe. Cant. viii.
scriptures: Gen 18:6
And Abraham hastened into the tent unto Sarah, and said, Make ready quickly three measures of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes upon the hearth.
And when the morning arose, then the angels hastened Lot, saying, Arise, take thy wife, and thy two daughters, which are here; lest thou be consumed in the iniquity of the city.
And she hasted, and emptied her pitcher into the trough, and ran again unto the well to draw water, and drew for all his camels.
Exo 5:13
And the taskmasters hasted them, saying, Fulfil your works, your daily tasks, as when there was straw.
corruption_summary: Hurry adopted as a way of life and mistaken for diligence — while the haste Scripture actually commends, running for the sake of a guest or a fugitive, is crowded out by it.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs has already distinguished what the modern schedule confuses: the thoughts of the diligent tend to plenteousness, but of every one that is hasty only to want. Constant hurry is not the same thing as productive urgency; it is usually its enemy, because a man in a permanent rush is unavailable for exactly the interruptions Genesis 18 is made of. Abraham was sitting in his tent door in the heat of the day when the three men appeared — unhurried, and therefore able to hurry when it mattered.

Genesis 19:15 supplies the other half, and it is sobering. The angels hastened Lot, and the next verse says he lingered, and they had to take him by the hand and bring him out. There are hours when delay is not prudence but peril, and the man in danger is usually the last to feel it. Scripture's counsel about the day of salvation has the same urgency — to day if ye will hear his voice — and the lingering man in Genesis is the standing picture of everyone who intends to attend to it later.
roots_summary: Hebrew mahar (H4116), to hurry, make haste — Abraham's word to Sarah; chush (H2363), to hasten, be eager; Greek speudo (G4692), to hasten — hasting unto the coming of the day of God.
roots_lines: Hebrew mahar (H4116) — to hasten, do quickly; Abraham hastening for his guests (Gen 18:6) and the angels hastening Lot (Gen 19:15).
Hebrew chush (H2363) — to hurry, be eager; I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments (Psa 119:60).
Greek speudo (G4692) — to hasten, be eager; Zacchaeus made haste and came down (Luk 19:6), and believers hasten unto the day of God (2Pe 3:12).
usage: “Abraham hastened into the tent… and he hasted to dress it” — an old man running for strangers.
“The angels hastened Lot” — and he lingered anyway.
“The taskmasters hasted them” — the same verb in the service of tyranny.
